435.title: The born-free and the rest of us (1.19–1.22)
435.hook: a few beings arrive at deep absorption by their very nature; for everyone else, Patanjali lists five things you need
435.howItsDone: Yoga teachers often present shraddha, virya, smriti, samadhi and prajna as qualities to cultivate over a lifetime, and point to 1.21 to say that sincere intensity matters more than natural gifts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sabija, samadhi with seed, absorption that still rests on something, and the kind that rests on nothing. With, without.

Every school has one. The kid who sits down at a piano at four and just plays. The one who never studied and still aced the test. It's easy to decide that some people have it and others don't. Patanjali noticed that too, in his own way. In sutra 1.19 he admits that some beings reach deep absorption by their very nature. Then, in 1.20, he turns to the rest of us, and doesn't sound worried at all.
screen: `THE KID WHO JUST PLAYS.` → `SOME HAVE IT, SOME DON'T?` → `PATANJALI TURNS TO THE REST OF US.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.19 names the born-free. For the bodiless ones and those merged in nature, the state arises from their very becoming: by birth, not effort. Who are they? The commentator Vyasa describes beings who have identified with the elements or with nature itself, and he adds a caution: their state looks like freedom, but it wears off, and they come back. So, in Vyasa's reading, the born-free aren't the goal. Sutra 1.20 is the main line. For everyone else, samadhi is preceded by five things: shraddha, faith, a settled trust that the path is real; virya, energy; smriti, memory or mindfulness, keeping the aim in view; samadhi itself, the gathering; and prajna, wisdom. Talent isn't on the list. Each of the five can be grown. Then 1.21: it is near for those whose urgency is intense. And 1.22 adds a wry detail: even among the intense, there's mild, medium and intense. Mild intensity, medium intensity, intense intensity. Commentators work out nine grades from these. It sounds like a scoreboard, but read it the other way round. One way to read it: in these sutras, how near the goal is depends on how much you care, not on what you were born with.
screen: `THE BORN-FREE: BY NATURE.` · `THE REST: FIVE THINGS TO GROW.` · `NEAR FOR THE INTENSE.` · then, large: `MILD, MEDIUM, INTENSE.`

segments.voice: Touch the five, a few breaths each: faith, any trust that sitting like this is worth it; energy, lengthen the spine and wake the body; memory, recall why you came to this practice. Then gather on the breath, and for wisdom, notice without judging how intense your wanting is today, mild, medium or intense. Any of them is a fine place to start.
Shraddha, faith, a settled trust the path is real, the first of five that lead to samadhi. A few reach absorption by nature; everyone else needs faith, energy, memory, gathering and wisdom.
Your line: mild, medium, intense. Tomorrow, one small word opens a second road. Day four hundred thirty-five.

436.title: Or — devotion to Ishvara (1.23–1.26)
436.hook: after all the talk of effort and intensity, Patanjali adds one small word, or, and opens a second road
436.tomorrow: Om is his name; repeat it; know its meaning
436.howItsDone: Many Hindu yoga lineages treat ishvara pranidhana as central, practiced through prayer, offering one's actions to God, and repeating a divine name, while others teach it as one of several supports for meditation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shraddha, faith, and the dial of mild, medium, intense. Today, a different road.
screen: `THE BORN-FREE AND THE REST OF US.`

segments.voice: Sutra after sutra, Patanjali has talked like a coach. Practice long, without breaks. Let go of thirst. Bring faith, energy, memory. Turn up the intensity. It's a lot of effort, and you might start to feel the weight of it. Then, in sutra 1.23, a tiny Sanskrit word: va. It means or. One syllable in either language, and it changes the whole tone. Or, the sutra says, there's another way.
screen: `PRACTICE. LET GO. TURN IT UP.` → `THEN ONE SMALL WORD.` → `VA: OR.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.23: ishvara pranidhanad va. Or, by devotion to Ishvara. Ishvara means the Lord. Pranidhana means placing yourself before, setting yourself down in front of: devotion, surrender, dedication. The commentator Vyasa explains why this is a shortcut. Through this special devotion, he says, the Lord turns toward the practitioner and favors them, by his will alone, and absorption becomes near. So this road isn't only your effort. It's met from the other side. Then, in three short sutras, Patanjali says who Ishvara is. 1.24: a special kind of purusha, a special seer, untouched by afflictions, by actions, by their fruits and by the traces they leave. 1.25: in Ishvara, the seed of all-knowing is unsurpassed. 1.26: the teacher even of the most ancient teachers, because Ishvara is not limited by time. Notice what's not said. Ishvara isn't described here as the creator of the world, and Patanjali doesn't name a particular god. Scholars debate how central Ishvara is to the whole text: some read Patanjali's yoga as deeply theistic, others as a method in which devotion is one powerful option among several. Hindu teachers in many lineages take it as a real invitation to bhakti, the word you met at the end of the Shvetashvatara. Either way, the sutra leaves a tired practitioner a second road, one that doesn't rest on effort alone. Or.

segments.voice: For the first part of this sit, try hard: return to the breath, alert, effortful. Halfway through, set yourself down, the way you'd set down a heavy bag, before God as you know God if you pray, or before the stillness itself if you don't. Let the effort soften, and notice what changes.
Or. The small word va in sutra 1.23 that opens a second road: devotion to Ishvara, the Lord, who meets the practitioner from the other side.
Your line: the shortcut. A road met from the other side. Day four hundred thirty-six, done.

437.title: Om is his name; repeat it; know its meaning (1.27–1.29)
437.hook: Patanjali gives the Lord of yesterday's sutra a name, and a three-part method for using it
437.howItsDone: Many Hindus repeat om or a divine name in japa, often on a mala, a string of beads, and teachers stress that the repetition should be joined with attention to the name's meaning, as Yoga Sutra 1.28 describes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: or, devotion to Ishvara, the shortcut, a road met from the other side. Today the Lord gets a name.

You've met om many times on this path. It opened year two, in the Chandogya, as the essence of essences. It was the bow in the Mundaka, the upper fire stick in the Shvetashvatara. So when Patanjali reaches it, you might expect a long hymn. Instead he gives it three sutras, crisp as a recipe: what om is, what to do with it, and what happens when you do.
screen: `THE ESSENCE OF ESSENCES.` → `THE BOW. THE FIRE STICK.` → `NOW: A RECIPE.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.27: tasya vachakah pranavah. The word that expresses him is the pranava. Pranava is the old name for om, the humming syllable. Vachaka means the word that names, the expression. So om is to Ishvara as a name is to a person. The commentator Vyasa adds that the link between this word and what it names isn't made up by convention; it's already there, and using the word simply brings it to light. Sutra 1.28: taj japas tad artha bhavanam. Its repetition, and dwelling on its meaning. Two parts. Japa: saying it again and again. Artha bhavana: letting its meaning soak in as you say it. The sutra keeps the two together: the sound, and the meaning held while it sounds. Sutra 1.29 gives the result. From that comes inward-turned awareness, and the obstacles disappear. So the name does two jobs: it turns attention toward the seer, and it clears the road. Tomorrow, those obstacles, all nine. You practiced japa in year one, with beads and a mantra; here is Patanjali's short description of it. It's simple enough for anyone: one syllable, repeated, with the heart behind it. If om isn't your word, many Hindu teachers say the same method works with whatever divine name a person holds dear.

segments.voice: On each out-breath, let om sound, aloud or silently, whichever suits where you are: that's japa. Pranava, the old name for om. Sutra 1.27: this word expresses Ishvara. Repeat it and dwell on its meaning, and the mind turns inward.
Your line: japa, again. The sound and its meaning, held together each time. See you tomorrow.

438.title: The nine obstacles (1.30–1.31)
438.hook: Patanjali lists, nearly two thousand years ago, exactly what goes wrong when people try to practice
438.howItsDone: Yoga teachers often have students learn the nine antarayas by name, so that illness, doubt or a plateau can be recognized as a normal part of practice rather than a reason to quit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pranava, om, the Lord's name. Japa, again, with its meaning, and the obstacles disappear. Today: which obstacles?

Day one of a new habit: you're on fire. Day four: a cold. Day six: you're tired and skip it. Day nine: you wonder if any of this works. Day twelve: a great session, so you assume you've arrived and stop paying attention. Day fifteen: the good feeling is gone and you can't get it back. Plenty of people who keep a practice know some version of this slide. Patanjali's list in sutra 1.30 reads like a map of it.
screen: `DAY ONE: ON FIRE.` → `A COLD. A SKIP. A DOUBT.` → `PATANJALI MAPS THE SLIDE.`

segments.voice: Here are the nine. Vyadhi: illness; the body gets sick and practice stops. Styana: dullness, a mind that won't get going. Samshaya: doubt, is this even real? Pramada: carelessness, not tending the conditions. Alasya: laziness, heaviness of body and mind. Avirati: craving, the pull of the senses that won't let go. Bhranti darshana: false seeing, mistaking one thing for another; one example is taking a good moment for arrival. Alabdha bhumikatva: not reaching a stage, the plateau where nothing seems to move. And anavasthitatva: reaching a stage and failing to hold it. Patanjali calls these the scatterings of the mind. Sutra 1.31 adds the companions that tend to come with them, four signs you can feel in the body: pain, dejection, trembling of the limbs, and ragged breathing in and out. Two things stand out. First, how ordinary the list is. Illness and laziness sit right next to doubt and false seeing. The obstacles aren't demons. They're Tuesday. Second, the last two are about progress: never reaching a new stage, and reaching it and slipping off. On this list, a good day can trip a practitioner up as easily as a bad one. Naming them doesn't make them vanish. But it changes the story from I'm bad at this to oh, that's number three, doubt. Tomorrow, the remedy.

segments.voice: Rest on the breath and watch for the nine as they show up: dullness like a heavy fog, doubt asking what's the point, craving with a sudden thought of food or your phone. Each time, name it kindly, the way you'd spot a bird, there's doubt, and come back to the breath. If the breath turns ragged or restless, name that too, and return.
Antaraya, obstacle, literally what comes in between. Patanjali names nine: illness, dullness, doubt, carelessness, laziness, craving, false seeing, failing to reach a stage, and failing to hold one.
Your line: not demons, just Tuesday. Nine obstacles, and each one has a name. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

439.title: One-pointed practice removes them (1.32)
439.hook: nine obstacles, and Patanjali's remedy fits in one short sutra: practice on one thing
439.howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers advise choosing one practice, one mantra or one form of the divine and staying with it for years, rather than switching methods, and they often cite Yoga Sutra 1.32 for this.

segments.voice: Yesterday: antaraya, the nine obstacles, from illness and doubt to plateaus and slipping. Not demons, just Tuesday. Today, the remedy.

A man needs water. He digs ten feet down in one corner of his field, finds dry dirt, and gives up. He digs ten feet somewhere else. Dry again. By the end of summer the field is full of shallow holes, and he's still carrying water up from the river. One hole, dug forty feet down, would have reached it. Patanjali has named nine obstacles. You might expect nine cures. He gives one, in a single short sutra, and it's that deep hole: one thing.
screen: `TEN SHALLOW HOLES, NO WATER.` → `ONE HOLE, DUG DEEP.` → `NINE OBSTACLES, ONE REMEDY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.32: tat pratishedhartham eka tattva abhyasah. To prevent them, practice on one principle. Tat, them: the obstacles. Pratishedha: warding off, keeping away. Eka: one. Tattva: a principle, literally thatness. Abhyasa: practice, the same word from five days ago, the steady return. So: to keep the scatterings away, return again and again to one thing. Which thing? The sutra doesn't say, and the commentators part ways. Vyasa reads it as any single object the mind is fixed on, one support instead of many. Others point to the sutras just before, about Ishvara and om, and read the one principle as the Lord. Both share a shape: stop spreading out. The obstacles feed on scattering. Doubt grows when you keep switching methods. Laziness grows when nothing is the main thing. Plateaus feel endless when you keep starting over somewhere new. Vyasa also describes a mind that is one-pointed, ekagra, fixed on a single object, and treats it as the ground where real absorption becomes possible. That's the one-pointed in today's title. And it's modest. Not one perfect thing, not the right thing. Just one thing, chosen and returned to. Starting tomorrow, the next sutras offer a list of possible one things. Today is the rule underneath them: pick one, and stay.

440.title: Friendliness, compassion, joy, equanimity (1.33)
440.hook: one sutra gives four attitudes for four kinds of people, and says the mind grows clear by them
440.howItsDone: Many yoga teachers present sutra 1.33 as a daily practice for relationships, consciously meeting the happy with friendliness, the suffering with compassion, the good with gladness and wrongdoers with equanimity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ekagra, one thing. The obstacles feed on scattering, so pick one, and stay. Today, a first candidate for that one thing.

Scroll through a feed for two minutes. A friend from school got engaged. A stranger lost their home in a flood. Someone you admire did something generous. Someone else did something cruel, and the comments are on fire. Four kinds of news, and each can tug a mind a different way: envy, overwhelm, cynicism, rage. Sutra 1.33 starts out there, with other people, four kinds of them.
screen: `AN ENGAGEMENT. A FLOOD.` → `A KINDNESS. A CRUELTY.` → `FOUR TUGS ON THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.33 pairs four attitudes with four kinds of people. Maitri, friendliness, toward the happy. Karuna, compassion, toward those who suffer. Mudita, gladness, toward the good. And upeksha, equanimity, toward those who do wrong. Cultivate these, the sutra says, and the mind becomes clear and settled: chitta prasadana, the mind made calm and bright, like water once the mud has settled. The pairing is precise. Commentators read friendliness toward the happy as the answer to envy: their good news isn't your loss. Compassion toward the suffering keeps you from looking away. Gladness toward the good is harder than it sounds: being glad when someone else does right, without needing to be the one who did it. And equanimity toward wrongdoers doesn't mean approving. It means not letting their wrong take over your mind. Some modern teachers call these the four locks and the four keys: each kind of person a lock, each attitude the key that fits. Buddhists know the same four qualities by another name, the brahma viharas, and practice them too. The Yoga Sutras place them right after one-pointed practice, the first of several things the mind can rest on. So your one thing doesn't have to be the breath. It can be a way of meeting people.

441.title: Or — the breath (1.34)
441.hook: the second door Patanjali offers into a clear mind is the one you're already walking through: the breath
441.tomorrow: or — a luminous object; or a sorrowless mind; or a great heart
441.howItsDone: Yoga teachers often introduce sutra 1.34 as a gentle lengthened exhale with a short pause, well before the fuller pranayama practices of the second chapter, and caution students never to strain the breath.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the four keys. Friendliness for the happy, compassion for the suffering, gladness for the good, equanimity for those who do wrong. Today closes the week.

Watch someone who's just had bad news. Before they say a word, they let out a long breath. A basketball player at the free-throw line: one slow exhale, then the shot. A child after crying: shaky breaths, a deep sigh, then quiet. Nobody taught them that. The body seems to know that a long breath out settles something. Sutra 1.34 is one line long, and it starts with the small word you met on day four hundred thirty-six: or.
screen: `BAD NEWS: A LONG BREATH OUT.` → `THE FREE THROW: ONE EXHALE.` → `THE BODY ALREADY KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.34, in paraphrase: or, by breathing out and holding the breath. The words are prachchhardana, breathing out, almost expelling, and vidharana, holding, keeping it out. It sits in a list of ways to clear the mind that began yesterday with the four keys. Notice the va again, or. Patanjali isn't saying everyone must do this. He's offering another door. The commentator Vyasa reads it as breathing the air out through the nostrils with deliberate effort, then keeping it out for a while, and he calls that holding pranayama, a word the second chapter takes much further. This lesson keeps it gentle: the out-breath lengthened, a short pause at the bottom, nothing strained. Why does it help? The sutra doesn't say. The three scenes in the hook hint at an answer: people already use a long breath out to settle themselves. Here it becomes a door for the mind. Now the week, from the top. Day one, the born-free and the rest of us. Day two, or, devotion to Ishvara. Day three, om is his name. Day four, the nine obstacles. Day five, one thing. Day six, the four keys. And today: or, the breath. A week of doors, each one a way back to stillness.
screen: `PRACHCHHARDANA: BREATHING OUT.` · `VIDHARANA: A PAUSE, HOLDING OUT.` · `GENTLE, NOT STRAINED.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `A WEEK OF DOORS.`

segments.voice: Let the breath be natural for a few rounds, then let each out-breath grow a little longer than the in-breath, slow and easy through the nose, with a moment's rest at the bottom before the next breath comes on its own. No forcing, no gasping; if you feel any strain, go back to normal breathing.
Or. In sutra 1.34, the second door to a clear mind: breathing out, and resting in the pause before the next breath.
Your line: or the breath. One more door, and it goes wherever you go. That's day four hundred forty-one, and a full week.
